title: Java List Sorting
learningObjectives: Sort a list with Collections.sort or List.sort.
Use natural ordering for comparable values.
Provide a Comparator for custom ordering.
Sort strings without confusing case or locale rules.
Use list sorting and common Collections algorithms, respecting the ordering precondition of binarySearch.

understand.concept: Java lists can be sorted in place. Collections.sort(list) and list.sort(comparator) arrange elements according to natural ordering or a supplied Comparator. Natural ordering for numbers is ascending and for strings is lexicographic. Comparator.comparing can sort objects by a selected property, and reversed can invert an ordering. Sorting changes the list itself; make a copy first if the original order must be preserved.
understand.whyItMatters: This topic helps Java developers select and use the right standard-library tools for java list sorting in maintainable applications.

explain.narrative:
For values with a natural order, call Collections.sort or List.sort(null). For custom rules, pass a Comparator such as Comparator.reverseOrder or Comparator.comparing. Use thenComparing to define tie-breakers. A comparator should be consistent and avoid subtraction-based integer comparisons that can overflow. Sorting is in place, so any other variable referring to the same list observes the changed order.

## Common Collections algorithms

The `Collections` utility class provides algorithms for lists and collections. Common methods include `binarySearch` for a sorted list, `reverse` to reverse list order, `shuffle` to randomize order, `frequency` to count equal occurrences, and `min` and `max` to find extreme elements. Binary search requires the list to be sorted according to the same ordering used for the search. Randomized shuffle output should not be used as a fixed expected sequence in a test.
